To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the substrates dUMP and NADPH bind to ThyX in the order dUMP, NADPH, CH2H4 folate, (ii) NADPH binding is essential for efficient FAD reduction, but dUMP binding is essential to prevent NADPH oxidization by O2, (iii) CH2H4FOLATE is a very efficient competitor of O2 for FADH2.

dUMP binding to the active site of ThyX from Parabursaria Chlorellavirus-1 accelerates NADPH reduction of FAD by over 4 orders of magnitude to 30 s-1 and, in the reverse direction, NADPH binding accelerates dUMP accommodation by 3-fold.

(a) the substrates of ThyX, NADPH, dUMP, and CH2H4 folate, interact with the protein and with each other, and (b) these interactions are essential for the efficient catalysis of dTMP synthesis, but they also prevent the protein to act as a NADPH oxidoreductase.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics of the active site and how the substrate interactions are controlled in ThyX, and how the active site is organized to avoid the formation of reactive oxygen species.
the dynamics of substrate interactions in the active site, and how this controls the wasteful oxidase activity of ThyX proteins.
understanding the dynamics of substrate interactions in a complex active site and the role of the native substrates in controlling the wasteful and potentially toxic O2 reaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ThyX reaction is a highly efficient and wasteful NADPH oxidoreductase that is only prevented from doing so by its substrates, which are not required for catalysis.
ThyX is a very efficient and highly selective dTMP biosynthesis catalyst, but not a wasteful NADPH oxidoreductase.
ThyX is a dUMP reductase that also acts as an NADPH oxidoreductase, but only when dUMP is present.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while ThyX is not a rate-limiting enzyme, it has a very important function in protecting cells from the potentially toxic effects of NADPH oxidases.
ThyX proteins are not only important for DNA replication, but they also play an important role in protecting cells from oxidative damage.
ThyX proteins, although they are present in aerobic microorganisms, are not NADPH oxidases but rather thymidylase enzymes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interplay of substrates in ThyX is crucial to avoid wasteful and potentially dangerous side reactions.

, despite the fact that the reaction mechanism of ThyX is very similar to that of the well-studied eukaryotic ThyA protein, the dynamic interplay of substrates is very different and may explain the different roles of these proteins in different organisms.
the substrate binding dynamics in ThyX proteins is crucial for their catalytic efficiency.
